identification.summary: Microsoft describes Storm-1175 as a financially motivated cybercriminal actor that runs high-velocity ransomware campaigns by weaponizing N-day (and occasionally zero-day) vulnerabilities in web-facing systems, then deploying Medusa ransomware [S1]. On 2026-08-02 Microsoft says it began deploying a new ransomware strain, StormEncryptor, its first activity seen by Microsoft since April 2026 [S4].
identification.firstObserved: Microsoft reports exploitation of web-facing assets by this actor since 2023 [S1]. The earliest dated indicator in Microsoft's IOC table is 2024-02-23 (SimpleHelp C2 IP) [S1].
identification.notes: Microsoft name: Storm-1175 (a Storm-#### designation for a developing cluster) [S1]. No other vendor aliases are stated in the sources gathered. Secondary reporting describes the actor as a former Medusa affiliate [S4]; Medusa itself runs a leak site for double extortion [S1]. Medusa ransomware as a family is distinct from this cluster, which is one actor that deploys it [S1].

attribution.sponsor: No state sponsor is stated. Microsoft characterizes the actor as a financially motivated cybercriminal actor [S1]. Secondary press (BleepingComputer, The Hacker News, Cloud Security Alliance) describes it as China-based or China-linked [S4][S5][S6].
attribution.confidence: The Microsoft April 2026 blog text retrieved does not state a country of origin [S1]. The China label appears in secondary coverage of Microsoft's reporting [S4][S6]; one CSA summary states the China label rests on operational and behavioral indicators rather than a confirmed link to the PLA or MSS [S5]. Treat geography as reported, not independently verified, and state nexus as unassessed.
attribution.basis: Microsoft telemetry and incident observations of exploitation, tooling and ransomware deployment [S1]. The basis for the China-based label is not shown in the sources retrieved.

objectives: Financial gain through data theft, double-extortion and encryption of victim networks with Medusa ransomware and, from August 2026, StormEncryptor [S1][S4].

targeting.notes: Microsoft says recent intrusions heavily affected healthcare organizations, plus education, professional services and finance in Australia, the UK and the US [S1]. Targeting is driven by exposed vulnerable internet-facing products rather than a named sector, so any organization running them is a candidate [S1]. The August 2026 N-able N-central exploitation implies managed-service and RMM-hosting environments are in scope [S4].

capabilities.summary: Rapid weaponization of recently disclosed flaws in internet-facing software; Microsoft lists more than 16 vulnerabilities exploited since 2023 across Exchange, PaperCut, Ivanti, ConnectWise ScreenConnect, JetBrains TeamCity, SimpleHelp, CrushFTP, GoAnywhere MFT, SmarterMail, BeyondTrust and SAP NetWeaver [S1]. Microsoft has seen at least three zero-days, two named: GoAnywhere MFT CVE-2025-10035 and SmarterMail CVE-2026-23760, exploited about a week before public disclosure [S1]. Time from access to exfiltration and ransomware is often a few days and sometimes within 24 hours [S1]. Persistence is by web shell or remote access payload and by creating a new administrator account [S1]. Lateral movement uses PowerShell, PsExec, RDP (enabling it via Windows Firewall changes if blocked), Impacket, renamed Cloudflare tunnels, PDQ Deployer and many RMM tools (Atera, Level, N-able, DWAgent, MeshAgent, ScreenConnect, AnyDesk, SimpleHelp) [S1]. Credential theft uses Impacket-based LSASS dumping, Mimikatz, WDigest enablement, a Veeam credential-recovery script, and NTDS.dit and SAM access [S1]. Defense evasion includes Microsoft Defender registry tampering and AV exclusions [S1]. Exfiltration uses Bandizip and Rclone [S1]. Medusa is typically launched through PDQ Deployer with a script named RunFileCopy.cmd, sometimes by Group Policy update [S1]. In August 2026 the actor deployed StormEncryptor, a C++ ransomware that appends .encrypted and drops a ransom note, detected by Microsoft as Ransom:Win64/StormEncryptor, alongside AnyDesk, SimpleHelp, Advanced IP Scanner and Mimikatz [S4].

campaigns.name: Early web-facing exploitation
campaigns.summary: Microsoft says the actor has exploited web-facing assets since 2023, including Exchange CVE-2022-41080/CVE-2022-41082 (OWASSRF, July 2023) and PaperCut CVE-2023-27350/27351 [S1].

campaigns.name: RMM-centric intrusions and WebLogic
campaigns.summary: Exploitation of Ivanti, ScreenConnect, TeamCity and SimpleHelp flaws is listed, with Oracle WebLogic exploitation in late 2024 (specific CVE not identified). Earliest dated IOCs are SimpleHelp C2 IPs from 2024-02-23 [S1].

campaigns.name: SAP NetWeaver CVE-2025-31324
campaigns.summary: Flaw disclosed 2025-04-24; Microsoft saw exploitation by this actor on 2025-04-25 [S1].

campaigns.name: GoAnywhere MFT CVE-2025-10035 (zero-day)
campaigns.summary: Microsoft lists GoAnywhere MFT CVE-2025-10035 among the zero-days exploited by this actor about a week before public disclosure [S1].

campaigns.name: Microsoft profile of high-tempo Medusa operations
campaigns.summary: Microsoft publishes a profile on 2026-04-06 including SmarterMail CVE-2026-23760 zero-day exploitation, BeyondTrust CVE-2026-1731, and heavy impact on healthcare in Australia, the UK and US [S1].

campaigns.name: StormEncryptor and suspected N-central exploitation
campaigns.summary: On 2026-08-02 Microsoft says the actor began deploying StormEncryptor, first activity since April 2026 and a shift from Medusa. Initial access likely involved N-able N-central CVE-2026-18577, though the exact vulnerability is unconfirmed [S4].

diamond.adversary: Financially motivated ransomware operator tracked by Microsoft as Storm-1175; reported by secondary sources as China-based [S1][S4][S6].
diamond.capability: N-day and occasional zero-day exploitation of web-facing products, RMM tooling abuse, Impacket/Mimikatz credential theft, Rclone exfiltration, Medusa then StormEncryptor ransomware [S1].
diamond.infrastructure: Web shells on exploited servers, SimpleHelp C2 servers (three IPs listed by Microsoft), Cloudflare tunnels, attacker-controlled cloud storage for Rclone sync [S1].
diamond.victim: Healthcare, education, professional services and finance organizations in Australia, UK and US running exposed vulnerable products [S1].
diamond.socioPolitical: Criminal extortion for profit; no state tasking is stated in Microsoft's text [S1]. Whether the actor has any link to the PRC state is unassessed in the sources [S5].
diamond.technology: Internet-facing file transfer, remote support, email, collaboration and RMM platforms, and Windows domain environments including Defender and PDQ Deployer [S1].

gaps: Microsoft's retrieved April 2026 blog text does not state a country of origin; the China-based label comes from secondary coverage and I could not open Microsoft's August 2026 post or the X thread in full [S1][S4].

Whether Storm-1175 is a Medusa affiliate or a separate operator that left Medusa is stated only in secondary press (BleepingComputer headline 'former Medusa affiliate'); I could not open the full articles [S4].
The third zero-day Microsoft mentions is not named in the retrieved text [S1].
Exact N-central vulnerability used in August 2026 is unconfirmed by Microsoft [S4].
Third-party names such as 'Spearwing' were not found in any source reviewed; no alias is added.
No government attribution, indictment, sanctions or MITRE ATT&CK group entry was found; the mitreGroupId field is empty.
Victim counts, ransom amounts and operator identities are not public in the sources gathered.
Could not open The Hacker News, Security Affairs or BleepingComputer pages directly (host unreachable); their content is taken from search summaries only.

Microsoft's October 2025 GoAnywhere blog and the Microsoft X post on StormEncryptor were not confirmed in search results and were removed as sources; their detail claims were removed or re-pointed to S1/S4.

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1: Key terrain is internet-facing file transfer, remote support, email and RMM platforms (GoAnywhere, SmarterMail, SimpleHelp, ScreenConnect, N-central) and the domain controllers and backup servers behind them [S1]. STEP 2: The actor is a criminal operator, not a state service, per Microsoft, so defense-sector exposure comes from contractor, healthcare (military health system partners) and managed-service dependencies rather than targeting of DoD by design [S1]. STEP 3: Template is exploit of a fresh vulnerability, often within days or before disclosure, then web shell or RMM install, new admin account, credential dumping, Rclone exfiltration, and Medusa or StormEncryptor via PDQ Deployer or Group Policy [S1]. STEP 4: MLCOA is continued opportunistic ransomware against organizations running newly disclosed vulnerable products, with 1-6 day dwell [S1]. MDCOA is exploitation of an RMM or MSP platform to reach many downstream customers, including defense contractors and base-supporting services, at once [S4]. Candidate indicators: unexpected RMM agents (SimpleHelp, MeshAgent, AnyDesk, Atera) on servers, renamed Cloudflare tunnel binaries, new local admin accounts, Defender exclusion or WDigest registry changes, Rclone use, RunFileCopy.cmd, .encrypted files [S1].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. (1) Situational awareness: track vendor advisories and CISA-style exploited-vulnerability notices for the products listed and treat the patch window as hours, since Microsoft saw next-day and pre-disclosure exploitation [S1]. (2) Authorities: patching, isolation of web-facing systems and RMM hunting on contractor or partner networks depend on owner authorities and DIB reporting channels; coordinate rather than assume control [S1]. (3) Mission assurance: prioritize backups, offline recovery and segmentation of file-transfer and RMM servers from mission systems, given 24-hour to 6-day time to ransomware [S1]. (4) Coordination: share indicators with DC3 and the DIB CS program and with healthcare and MSP partners; because attribution to a state is unestablished, route as criminal ransomware incidents [S1][S5].

provenance.importedSummary: Storm-1175 is a cybercriminal group known for deploying Medusa ransomware and exploiting public-facing applications for initial access. They have been observed exploiting a critical deserialization vulnerability in GoAnywhere MFT, tracked as CVE-2025-10035, which could lead to command injection and potential RCE. Microsoft Defender researchers identified exploitation activity aligned with TTPs attributed to Storm-1175, including the use of post-compromise techniques that involve creating a group named “ESX Admins” in the domain.
